reason: The only observations are a service_name 'psexesvc' deletion event on host file-srv-02 by user jdavis at a timestamp (obs_7ecafc53b93d, obs_de45e2cca4cc, obs_22b885f4ba96, obs_ef921ba616aa). PSEXESVC is the ephemeral service created by PsExec for remote command execution, and its deletion following use is routine cleanup of a transient execution artifact rather than removal of an established persistence mechanism; no observation shows this service was configured for persistence (e.g., auto-start across reboots, being present prior to a related execution chain) or that any file, registry, or account artifact tied to persistence was removed. Clear Persistence (T1070.009) requires evidence of a previously established persistence mechanism, which is absent here -- that would require a prior EVT record showing the service configured to survive reboot/logon or another persistence artifact predating this deletion, and no such record is cited. File Deletion (T1070.004) does not apply because only a service object, not a file, was deleted (no file path or filesystem deletion event is present). No other candidate's defining behavior (log/history clearing, timestomping, network share removal, masquerading, tool injection, mailbox clearing) is demonstrated by a service-name and deletion timestamp alone. Abstaining is appropriate given the ephemeral-service caveat and lack of supporting persistence evidence.

The observations only show a network-layer connection record (src_ip 10.0.1.10 to dst_ip 10.0.1.22 on tcp/445, allowed by firewall rule 'allow-int-smb') with byte counts. There is no evidence of authenticated SMB session establishment, file/share access, admin share usage, file transfer content, exploitation, or any credential/protocol-specific action that would confirm SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) or Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) or any other candidate. A connection allowed on port 445 alone does not demonstrate the defining behaviour of authenticated share interaction or file copy; that would require session/auth logs (e.g., SMB tree connect, file read/write events) which are not present in EVT-0231. Abstaining rather than substituting a related but unproven technique.

The observation set (EVT-0232) records only a Windows service creation event on FILE-SRV-02 (service_name='psexesvc', service_path='psexesvc.exe', hostname='file-srv-02', username='jdavis', timestamp) — a local service-installation artifact. None of the candidate techniques' defining behaviours (e.g., SMB/Windows Admin Shares requires evidence of an authenticated SMB session or admin-share file copy; WinRM requires WinRM protocol use; DCOM requires COM activation; Remote Services/Use Alternate Authentication Material require evidence of the actual remote logon mechanism) are demonstrated by a service-create record alone. Per the guidance, a service-create record alone is not proof of SMB share access or any specific remote-access protocol; the SMB session, WinRM call, or credential material that would normally accompany PsExec-style lateral movement would appear in network/auth logs (e.g., SMB session establishment or 4624 logon type 3 events), which are not present in the cited observations. Abstaining rather than substituting a related but unproven mechanism.

The observations show a successful network logon by jdavis from wkstn-07 to auth-srv-01 (EVT-0228: username='jdavis', source_host='wkstn-07', dest_host='auth-srv-01', logon_type='network', result='success') plus an unrelated endpoint event referencing lsass.exe/powershell.exe process activity (EVT-0226). None of the candidate techniques' defining behaviours are demonstrated: there is no evidence of a stolen password hash, Kerberos ticket, application token, or web session cookie being used (T1550 and its sub-techniques require observed credential material reuse, not just a successful network logon); there is no evidence of hijacking an existing session (T1563, T1563.001, T1563.002 require commandeering a pre-existing session, not establishing a new logon); there is no SMB share access, file transfer, tainted content, or vulnerability exploitation evident (T1021.002, T1570, T1080, T1210); and there is no cloud service authentication (T1021.007). A plain successful network logon record alone, even alongside an lsass.exe/powershell.exe process event, does not establish which authentication material or mechanism was used, so no technique's defining behaviour is supported by the cited fields.
